fep-5a4740c29cc82303-qC1:a.hint: Draw the energy entering from the hot reservoir, the useful work and the energy rejected to the cold reservoir.
notes: Over a complete engine cycle ΔU = 0, so W = Q_hot − Q_cold and efficiency = W/Q_hot. Use energy per cycle or power consistently.
Only an ideal reversible Carnot engine reaches η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot. Both reservoir temperatures must be in kelvin; this gives an upper bound for a real engine.

duplicate-600962388ff5703d.hint: Translate “isothermal” into a statement about temperature, then consider what that means for an ideal gas’s internal energy.
notes: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, ΔU = 0 and therefore Q = W using work done by the gas. A fixed amount obeys pV = constant.
No temperature change does not mean no heat transfer. Heat can enter during expansion to replace the energy transferred out as work.

duplicate-8c1257e6fa252c42.hint: Which energy-transfer route is excluded by “adiabatic”? Apply the first law with that term removed.
notes: Adiabatic means Q = 0, so ΔU = −W when W is work done by the gas. Expansion can cool the gas; compression can warm it.
For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process, pV^γ is constant (γ = C_p/C_v). Do not replace this with pV = constant, which belongs to an isothermal process.

fep-5a4740c29cc82303-qC1:a.text: A heat engine takes energy from a hot reservoir, converts some into work and rejects the rest to a cold reservoir. A heat pump uses supplied work to transfer energy from a colder reservoir to a warmer one. Their useful outputs are different: work for the engine, transferred thermal energy for the pump.

fep-02c159d8c1e97420-qC2:d.iii.text: The efficiency is approximately 1 − 473/673 = 0.297. From 1000 J of heat input the engine delivers about 300 J of work, so the heat rejected is Qout = Qin − W ≈ 1000 − 300 = 700 J.

fep-9c2d0cebe79d4071-qC2:d.iii.text: The efficiency is approximately 1 − 473/673 = 0.297. From 1000 J of heat input the engine delivers about 300 J of work, so the heat rejected is Qout = Qin − W ≈ 1000 − 300 = 700 J.

fep-166845b0058d8d48-qC1:a.text: Draw thermal energy QC flowing from the room into the heat pump, work W flowing from the motor into the pump, and thermal energy QH flowing from the pump to the outside air. The QH arrow is the largest, since QH = QC + W.

fep-166845b0058d8d48-qC1:b.text: Conservation of energy gives QH = QC + W: the energy delivered outside equals the energy removed from the room plus the work supplied to the pump.

fep-166845b0058d8d48-qC1:c.text: Yes. The thermal energy removed from the room can exceed the work supplied. The pump transfers existing thermal energy rather than converting work alone into the entire heat output; QH = QC + W still holds.

fep-166845b0058d8d48-qC1:d.text: For the ideal reversible pump, QC/W = Tc/(Th − Tc) = 280/(320 − 280) = 7. With 500 W of input power, the maximum rate of thermal energy removal is 7 × 500 = 3500 W.

fep-166845b0058d8d48-qC1:e.text: There is no violation: work is supplied to move thermal energy from the colder room to the warmer outside air. The second law forbids this transfer as the sole result of a process, without another change. The total entropy of room, surroundings and power supply does not decrease.
